title: Pods and Workload Controllers
description: Understand how Pods are the smallest deployable units in Kubernetes and how workload controllers like Deployments, StatefulSets, and DaemonSets manage them in production.

data.text: A **Pod** is the smallest and simplest unit in the Kubernetes object model that you create or deploy. It represents a single instance of a running process in your cluster. Pods contain one or more containers (such as Docker containers), storage resources, and a unique network IP. Think of a Pod as a logical host — similar to a physical machine or a VM in the non-container world — but much lighter and meant to run a single application.

Pods are designed to be **ephemeral**. They do not heal themselves if they fail, and they are not meant to persist. If a Pod dies, Kubernetes creates a replacement — but that replacement is a brand new Pod with a new identity. This is why you rarely create Pods directly; instead, you use workload controllers that manage Pods for you.

Workload controllers are the brain of Kubernetes operations. They watch the current state of your cluster and continuously work to move it toward the desired state you declared. If a Pod crashes, a node fails, or you want to scale up during a traffic spike, the controller handles it automatically.

terms.definition: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, containing one or more containers.
A controller that manages stateless Pods and supports rolling updates.
A controller for stateful applications requiring stable network identities and persistent storage.
A controller that ensures a Pod runs on every (or selected) node in the cluster.
The controller Deployment uses to maintain a stable set of Pod replicas.

data.text: A **Deployment** gives you declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. It is the workhorse for stateless applications like APIs, web servers, and microservices. When you create a Deployment, Kubernetes creates a ReplicaSet, which in turn creates the actual Pods.

data.title: Deploying a web API with a Deployment
data.content: Create a Deployment that maintains three replicas of an API service.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-deployment
  labels:
    app: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myregistry.io/api:2.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080

data.title: Use Deployments for stateless apps
data.text: If your application does not need stable network IDs or persistent storage, use a Deployment. It handles rolling updates, rollbacks, and scaling automatically.

A **StatefulSet** is for applications that require stable, unique network identifiers and stable persistent storage. Databases like PostgreSQL, MySQL, and message queues like Kafka are common use cases. Unlike Deployments, StatefulSets assign a persistent name to each replica (e.g., `web-0`, `web-1`) that survives restarts.

data.title: StatefulSet for a database cluster
data.content: Deploy a 3-replica StatefulSet with persistent volume claims.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  serviceName: "postgres"
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:16
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
          name: postgres
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: data
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 20Gi

data.text: A **DaemonSet** ensures that a copy of a Pod runs on all (or a subset of) nodes in a cluster. This is perfect for node-level utilities like log collectors, monitoring agents, or network proxies. As new nodes join the cluster, the DaemonSet automatically schedules the Pod onto them.

data.title: DaemonSet for a log collector
data.content: Run Fluentd on every node to collect container logs.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluentd
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      name: fluentd
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        name: fluentd
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: fluentd
        image: fluent/fluentd:v1.16
        volumeMounts:
        - name: varlog
          mountPath: /var/log
      volumes:
      - name: varlog
        hostPath:
          path: /var/log

cards.title: Deployment
cards.description: For stateless apps that can scale horizontally.

cards.title: StatefulSet
cards.description: For stateful apps needing stable identity and storage.

cards.title: DaemonSet
cards.description: For node-level tasks that must run on every node.
cons: Runs on every node by default

data.title: Deploy a stateless API and a DaemonSet
data.description: Practice creating Deployments and DaemonSets in a cluster.
steps: Create a Deployment named "web-api" with 3 replicas using the nginx image.
Scale the Deployment to 5 replicas and observe the new Pods.
Create a DaemonSet named "node-exporter" that runs on every node.
Verify the DaemonSet Pods are running on all nodes with kubectl get pods -o wide.
Delete one DaemonSet Pod and watch Kubernetes recreate it automatically.
data.expectedOutcome: You understand when to use each controller and how Kubernetes maintains the desired state.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Pods are ephemeral and rarely created directly — controllers manage them.
Deployments are the default for stateless applications and support rolling updates.
StatefulSets provide stable identities and persistent storage for stateful workloads.
DaemonSets ensure a Pod runs on every node for node-level tasks.
Choose the right controller based on whether your workload is stateless, stateful, or node-level.
data.takeaway: Controllers abstract Pod lifecycle management, letting you declare intent rather than micromanage instances.
